title: ABRAHAM HAD SARAH. THEN HE HAD HAGAR. BUT DID ANYONE EVER ASK HAGAR IF SHE HAD A CHOICE?
paragraphs: ABRAHAM HAD SARAH. THEN HE HAD HAGAR. BUT DID ANYONE EVER ASK HAGAR IF SHE HAD A CHOICE?

She was an enslaved Egyptian woman caught between a desperate wife, a powerful husband, and a promise from God. Her body became someone else's solution. Her suffering became someone else's family conflict. But when everyone else saw a servant, heaven saw a woman worth calling by name.
What if one of the most overlooked women in Genesis has something to say to every person who has ever been used, abandoned, blamed, or made to suffer for a decision they never got to make?
There is a kind of pain that comes from making a terrible decision and living with the consequences.
But there is another kind of pain.
The kind that comes when somebody else makes the decision, and you are the one left bleeding.
You never agreed to the arrangement. You never asked to be placed in that position. You never volunteered to carry the consequences.
But somehow, when everything falls apart, everybody looks at you as though you are the problem.
If you have ever been there, you need to meet a woman named Hagar.
Not the sanitized version we sometimes hear in Bible stories. Not merely the servant who gave Abraham another son. Not simply the woman whose child became part of a complicated family history.
The real Hagar.
An Egyptian woman living in a household where other people possessed the power to decide what happened to her.
A woman whose story forces us to ask an uncomfortable question:
Abraham had Sarah. Then he had Hagar. But did Hagar ever have the freedom to say no?
And before we answer too quickly, we need to open our Bibles.
Because Scripture tells a story far more disturbing, far more human, and ultimately far more revealing of God's mercy than many of us realize.
Genesis 16 begins with a painful silence.
God had promised Abram descendants. The years had passed. Sarai remained childless.
Imagine the prayers.
The waiting.
The disappointment that returned month after month.
Imagine watching the calendar change while the promise appeared to stand still.
Sarai was not simply impatient. She was living with the deep sorrow of infertility in a culture where bearing children carried enormous social significance.
That sorrow deserves compassion.
But compassion for Sarai's suffering must never require us to overlook what happened to Hagar.
Because sometimes wounded people wound other people.
Sometimes the person who has been waiting for a miracle becomes so desperate to manufacture one that somebody else pays the price.
Genesis 16:2 records Sarai telling Abram, in the King James Version:
"Go in unto my maid; it may be that I may obtain children by her."
Read that again.
Not because the words are difficult.
Because the person missing from the conversation matters.
Sarai speaks.
Abram listens.
A plan is proposed.
But where is Hagar's voice?
The biblical account records no conversation in which Hagar is asked whether she wants this arrangement.
No statement of her consent.
No indication that she possesses the same freedom to accept or refuse as the people deciding her future.
That does not mean we can reconstruct every private conversation that occurred. Scripture does not tell us everything.
But what Scripture does tell us is enough to make us uncomfortable.
Genesis 16:1 identifies Hagar as Sarai's Egyptian שִׁפְחָה — shiphchah, a Hebrew term for a female servant or enslaved woman.
This was not an equal relationship between independent adults.
Hagar occupied a subordinate position in Sarai's household.
Then Genesis 16:3 says Sarai took Hagar and gave her to Abram as a wife.
The Hebrew uses אִשָּׁה — ishshah, meaning "woman" or "wife," depending on context.
That detail matters.
Hagar was given a marital status within the arrangement, but the text does not tell us that her subordinate status disappeared or that she became equal to Sarai.
And the verb matters too.
Sarai took her.
Sarai gave her.
Abram went in to her.
Hagar conceived.
The narrative records the actions of those with authority and the pregnancy that followed.
It does not record Hagar choosing the arrangement.
We should not pretend to know the words she might have spoken in private.
But neither should we invent a willing agreement that the biblical text never provides.
A woman can be described as a wife and still lack meaningful power over the circumstances that brought her into the relationship.
This is where the story begins to challenge the way we read the Bible.
Because Abraham is a towering figure of faith.
And rightly so.
God called him. God made covenant promises to him. The New Testament honors his faith.
But being chosen by God did not make every decision Abraham made righteous.
The Bible does not teach that its heroes were flawless.
It reveals the faithfulness of God through deeply imperfect people.
And if we turn every action of a biblical patriarch into an example to imitate, we will end up defending things Scripture never commands us to defend.
The fact that Genesis describes this arrangement does not mean God prescribed it.
The fact that it occurred within an ancient household does not mean it expressed God's ideal for marriage, dignity, or justice.
Jesus later pointed back to creation when teaching about marriage, saying that the two become one flesh (Matthew 19:4–6).
The original creation account presents man and woman together as bearers of God's image (Genesis 1:27).
Hagar's story takes place in a fallen world where power, desperation, household hierarchy, and human attempts to secure the future collide.
And when they collide, the vulnerable are often the first to suffer.
Then something happens.
Hagar becomes pregnant.
The plan appears to work.
But the household does not become peaceful.
Genesis 16:4 says that when Hagar saw she had conceived, her mistress became despised in her eyes.
We must not erase that verse.
Scripture does not portray Hagar as incapable of wrongdoing simply because she was vulnerable.
Her attitude toward Sarai became part of the conflict.
But neither does that justify what followed.
Sarai blamed Abram.
Abram handed responsibility back to Sarai.
And Genesis 16:6 records his words:
"Behold, thy maid is in thy hand; do to her as it pleaseth thee."
Think about the weight of that sentence.
The man who had participated in the arrangement now left Hagar under Sarai's authority.
The woman who had been brought into the household's plan became the object of its anger.
And Sarai dealt harshly with her.
The Hebrew verb used in Genesis 16:6 comes from עָנָה — anah, which in this form conveys afflicting, oppressing, or treating someone harshly.
This was not merely an awkward family disagreement.
The biblical language describes mistreatment.
And Hagar fled.
Pregnant.
Away from the household.
Into the wilderness.
We do not know every thought running through her mind.
We do not know whether she feared for her life, what provisions she carried, or exactly what future she imagined.
But we know she left.
And that single fact should stop us.
Because the arrangement that was supposed to solve someone else's problem had become so painful that the woman carrying the child ran away.
Perhaps that is where this story finds you.
You were useful when somebody needed something.
You were welcomed when you could solve a problem.
You were praised when you could carry a burden.
But when the relationship became complicated, when the promise became inconvenient, when the people in power needed someone to blame, suddenly you were disposable.
Maybe it happened in your family.
Maybe in a relationship.
Maybe in a workplace.
Maybe even in a religious community where people knew how to speak about God but did not know how to treat you with dignity.
And the question that kept you awake was not merely, "Why did they hurt me?"
It was something deeper.
"Did anybody see what happened to me?"
Hagar's story answers that question in a way that still reaches across thousands of years.
Because the wilderness was not the end of her story.
Genesis 16:7 says:
"And the angel of the LORD found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness."
Found her.
Do not rush past those two words.
The household had become a place of oppression.
The wilderness was a place of uncertainty.
But the messenger of the LORD found Hagar there.
The text does not say Hagar had finally become important enough to be noticed.
It does not say she earned God's attention by performing some extraordinary act of faith.
It simply tells us that she was found.
Then comes one of the most remarkable moments in the chapter.
Genesis 16:8:
"Hagar, Sarai's maid, whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go?"
He calls her Hagar.
By name.
In a story where people have repeatedly spoken about her, acted upon her, and made decisions involving her, the divine messenger addresses her directly.
"Hagar."
Not merely a servant.
Not merely a womb.
Not merely the source of household tension.
Hagar.
A person.
Someone with a past.
Someone facing an uncertain future.
Someone whose suffering has not escaped heaven's attention.
And she answers.
"I flee from the face of my mistress Sarai."
There it is.
Her own voice.
Her own account of what is happening.
And what follows is not an easy passage.
The angel of the LORD tells Hagar to return to her mistress and submit herself under her authority.
We must handle this verse carefully.
Because Scripture has sometimes been misused to pressure abused or exploited people into returning to dangerous situations.
Genesis 16:9 is part of a particular encounter in a particular ancient setting. It is not a universal command telling every mistreated person to remain under an abuser's control.
God's recorded instruction to Hagar must not be turned into a weapon against someone seeking safety.
The passage does not give us permission to minimize oppression, deny protection, or silence people who need help.
In fact, the very next verse reveals something astonishing.
God has not come merely to send Hagar back into the household.
He speaks a promise over her future.
Genesis 16:10 says:
"I will multiply thy seed exceedingly, that it shall not be numbered for multitude."
Consider who is receiving that promise.
An Egyptian servant woman.
A foreigner.
A person whose social position offered little security.
Yet she is addressed with a promise concerning her descendants.
Then Genesis 16:11 announces that she will bear a son.
His name will be Ishmael.
In Hebrew, יִשְׁמָעֵאל — Yishma'el means "God hears" or "God has heard."
And the reason given is deeply personal:
"Because the LORD hath heard thy affliction."
Not because Hagar was powerful.
Not because she belonged to the favored side of the household.
Not because her circumstances were easy to explain.
Because God heard her affliction.
The same chapter that describes Sarai's harsh treatment of Hagar also records heaven acknowledging Hagar's suffering.
God does not need to pretend her pain is insignificant in order to continue His covenant purposes.
And neither should we.
Then Hagar responds with words that make this story unforgettable.
Genesis 16:13 says:
"Thou God seest me."
The Hebrew expression is אֵל רֳאִי — El Ro'i, traditionally rendered "God who sees me" or "God of seeing."

The exact nuance of the expression has been discussed by Hebrew scholars, but its central significance in the narrative is clear: Hagar recognizes that the God who addressed her has seen her in her distress.
And here is the beauty.
Hagar was not the person through whom God had promised the covenant line that would eventually lead to the Messiah.
But she was not invisible to Him.
She was not outside His concern.
She was not too foreign, too powerless, or too complicated to receive divine attention.
God's particular covenant purpose through Abraham and Sarah did not cancel His compassion for Hagar and Ishmael.
Somebody needs to hear that.
Being overlooked by people does not mean you have been overlooked by God.
Being mistreated by someone who speaks about God does not mean God approves of what they did.
Being caught in another person's failure does not mean your life has lost its worth.
But the story is not finished.
Years pass.
Isaac is born.
The promised son arrives through Sarah, just as God had said.
And the tension in Abraham's household returns.
Genesis 21 records another painful separation.
Sarah sees Ishmael, Hagar's son, in a way that troubles her, and she demands that Abraham send Hagar and Ishmael away.
Genesis 21:10 says:
"Cast out this bondwoman and her son."
The Hebrew term here is אָמָה — amah, another word used for a female servant or enslaved woman.
Notice what this reveals.
Even after Hagar bore Abraham's son, the narrative still describes her through the language of servitude.
Motherhood had not erased the unequal power surrounding her.
Abraham is distressed, particularly because Ishmael is his son.
God tells Abraham to heed Sarah regarding the covenant line through Isaac, while also promising that Ishmael will become a nation because he too is Abraham's offspring.
That distinction matters.
God's covenant with Isaac is not a declaration that Ishmael is worthless.
Nor is God's involvement in the separation an invitation for us to celebrate Hagar's distress.
Genesis 21 does not invite us to look at a suffering mother and say, "Well, everything worked out."
It invites us to see that God's purposes continue even through a household marked by human conflict.
Abraham gives Hagar bread and a skin of water.
She departs.
And once again, she is in the wilderness.
This time she is not alone.
Her son is with her.
And the water runs out.
There are few things more terrifying than a parent who cannot provide what a child needs to survive.
Hagar places the boy beneath a shrub and moves away because she cannot bear to watch him die.
Genesis 21:16 records her words:
"Let me not see the death of the child."
Then she weeps.
There is no need to embellish that scene.
The Bible has already given us enough to break our hearts.
A mother.
A child.
No water.
No visible rescue.
And a cry that comes from the terrible possibility of losing someone she loves.
If you are a parent who has ever watched your child suffer and felt helpless, you may understand something of that terror.
If you have ever reached the end of your resources, when no amount of determination could manufacture what you needed, you may recognize that wilderness.
And if you have ever wondered whether God still hears when you have no beautiful prayer left, listen carefully.
Genesis 21:17 says:
"And God heard the voice of the lad."
Again, the name Ishmael becomes significant.
God hears.
Not as an empty slogan.
Not as a guarantee that every crisis will resolve exactly as we want.
But as a truth demonstrated within the story.
The boy's suffering has not gone unnoticed.
God calls to Hagar from heaven.
He tells her not to fear.
He reaffirms His promise concerning Ishmael.
And then Genesis 21:19 says:
"And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water."
What a moment.
The text does not explain whether the well had previously been hidden from her sight or whether God enabled her to recognize what she had not seen.
We should not invent an explanation.
But we can see what the narrative emphasizes.
Hagar receives the help she needs.
She fills the skin with water.
She gives her son a drink.
And Ishmael lives.
The wilderness did not get the final word.
Despair did not get the final word.
The story did not end with a mother watching her child die.
And then comes a sentence we should never forget.
Genesis 21:20:
"And God was with the lad."
Not merely with Isaac.
God was also with Ishmael.
This does not erase the distinct covenant promises made through Isaac.
But it does confront the idea that those outside the covenant line were therefore beyond God's care.
The God of Abraham was not indifferent to the Egyptian mother and her son.
Now we need to ask an even deeper question.
Why does the Bible preserve this story?
Why allow us to see the uncomfortable decisions of people who would become central figures in the history of faith?
Why record the harsh treatment?
The running away?
The desperate crying?
Why not present Abraham and Sarah in a more flattering light?
Because the Bible is not a public relations campaign for its human characters.
It is a revelation of God's work in a world damaged by sin.
And sin is not always spectacular.
Sometimes sin looks like using another person to accomplish something we desperately want.
Sometimes it looks like refusing to take responsibility when our decisions hurt someone.
Sometimes it looks like allowing our own suffering to become an excuse for cruelty.
Sometimes it looks like religious people defending what is convenient rather than asking what is right.
Abraham's household had received extraordinary promises.
But extraordinary promises did not make its members incapable of ordinary human failure.
And that should humble every one of us.
Because there may be moments when we recognize ourselves in Hagar.
But there may also be moments when we recognize ourselves in Sarai.
We may have been hurt.
We may have waited.
We may have carried disappointments nobody else understood.
And yet, in our frustration, we may have treated someone else unfairly.
Or perhaps we recognize ourselves in Abram.
We knew something was wrong.
We had the opportunity to act.
But we chose the easier path of avoiding responsibility.
That is why this story cannot end with us merely deciding which character we like most.
It must bring us before God.
The God who sees the wounded also sees the ways we wound others.
The God who hears the afflicted also hears the excuses we make.
And the same God who calls us to acknowledge injustice calls us to repentance for the injustice we have committed.
This is where the story begins to point beyond itself.
Toward Jesus Christ.
Not because Hagar is secretly Jesus.
Not because every detail of her story should be forced into a hidden prediction of the cross.
But because the God whose compassion is revealed in Genesis is the God whose saving grace is revealed supremely in His Son.
Jesus did not enter a world of perfectly behaved religious people.
He entered a world of sinners.
A world where people were rejected.
A world where power was abused.
A world where women were often dismissed.
A world where the poor, the sick, the outcast, and the morally compromised could be treated as though their stories were already over.
And Jesus repeatedly challenged that assumption.
In John 4, He spoke with a Samaritan woman at a well.
A woman whose life carried complicated relational history.
A woman whom Jesus addressed directly, seriously, and truthfully.
He did not ignore the truth about her life.
But neither did He treat her as unworthy of receiving the truth about Himself.
He spoke of living water.
He revealed Himself as the Messiah.
And the woman who came to the well left speaking to others about Him.
Do not miss the connection.
Hagar's wilderness encounter and the Samaritan woman's encounter with Jesus are distinct events with different theological purposes.
But both narratives reveal something precious about God's character.
People whom society might overlook are not beyond His attention.
And in Jesus Christ, we see God's mercy and truth embodied in a way that calls sinners to salvation.
Jesus did not come merely to make people feel noticed.
He came to save.
The Gospel is greater than emotional validation.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for our sins, was buried, and rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
At the cross, the seriousness of sin is exposed.
And the greatness of God's grace is displayed.
We are not saved because we have suffered.
We are not saved because we have been treated unfairly.
We are not saved because our personal story is heartbreaking.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ (Ephesians 2:8–9).
The wounded need His grace.
The guilty need His forgiveness.
The proud need His correction.
The broken need His restoring power.
And every one of us needs the Savior.
That is why the story of Hagar should do more than move us emotionally.
It should change the way we see people.
It should make us slower to judge someone whose circumstances we do not understand.
It should make us more careful about how we use authority.
It should make us more willing to listen when someone says they have been mistreated.
It should make us question the habit of protecting respected people while dismissing those who lack influence.
And it should remind us that genuine faith never gives us permission to treat human beings as disposable.
James 1:27 speaks of caring for orphans and widows in their affliction.
James 2 warns against favoritism.
Jesus teaches His followers to love their neighbors.
These are not optional decorations added to faith.
They are part of what it means for faith to bear fruit.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes personal in a way you did not expect.
Maybe you are reading this because you feel like Hagar.
You were drawn into a situation you did not control.
You suffered consequences you did not choose.
You were blamed for a problem that was never yours alone.
And after everything, you found yourself asking whether your life still mattered.
Hear what Scripture actually allows us to say.
God sees suffering.
God hears the afflicted.
God cares about those who are vulnerable.
And through Jesus Christ, He offers forgiveness, reconciliation with Himself, and the hope of eternal life.
That does not mean every person who mistreated you will apologize.
It does not mean every broken relationship must be restored.
It does not mean you should return to an unsafe situation to prove you have faith.
Forgiveness does not require pretending evil was good.
Reconciliation requires truth, and restored trust may require repentance, accountability, and genuine change.
You can pursue healing without denying what happened.
You can seek safety without abandoning your faith.
And you can bring your pain before Christ without making your pain the whole definition of who you are.
But perhaps you are reading this and realizing you have been the one who used somebody.
You called it necessity.
You called it a misunderstanding.
You told yourself you had no choice.
You justified your behavior because you were hurting too.
Yet somewhere inside, you know another person paid a price for your decision.
Then the invitation is different.
Repent.
Not merely feel bad.
Not merely post something religious.
Turn away from the wrongdoing.
Tell the truth.
Accept responsibility.
Where possible and appropriate, make restitution.
Seek forgiveness without demanding it.
And let the grace of Jesus Christ transform not only what you believe but how you treat people.
Because Christianity is not about defending our favorite biblical characters at all costs.
It is about following the Lord Jesus Christ.
And the Lord Jesus Christ is not threatened by our willingness to acknowledge human sin.
He came because sin is real.
He died because forgiveness is costly.
He rose because death would not have the final word.
And He calls us to follow Him in truth.
There is one more thing we must understand about Hagar's story.
The New Testament returns to Hagar and Sarah in Galatians 4:21–31.
Paul uses the two women in an allegorical argument concerning slavery, freedom, and the distinction between seeking righteousness through the law and receiving the promise of God.
That passage has a specific theological purpose.
It should not be confused with a complete moral evaluation of Hagar's personal experience in Genesis.
Paul's argument does not require us to deny her suffering.
Nor does it turn Hagar into a villain.
And it certainly does not teach that God was indifferent to her.
In Genesis, Hagar is a real woman whose affliction God heard.
In Galatians, Paul draws a theological comparison involving the two women and their sons.
Responsible Bible reading respects both contexts.
And responsible Bible reading also remembers that Ishmael's descendants are not to be treated with contempt because of their ancestry.
The Gospel is not an invitation to despise peoples or nations.
Christ's commission extends to all nations.
The saving invitation is to repent and believe in Him.
That is the message we must never lose.
Not Abraham as our ultimate hero.
Not Sarah as our ultimate example.
Not Hagar as our ultimate redeemer.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
Abraham needed Him.
Sarah needed Him.
Hagar needed God's saving grace just as every human being does.
And so do we.
Now think about the title of this story one last time.
Abraham had Sarah.
Then he had Hagar.
But was Hagar ever given a real choice?
The most faithful answer is this:
Genesis does not record Hagar being asked for or giving her consent, and her enslaved status makes it deeply questionable whether she possessed meaningful freedom to refuse.
We must not claim to know private conversations Scripture does not reveal.
But we must not use that silence to excuse the unequal power the text clearly describes.
And perhaps the most remarkable thing about the story is that, while human beings repeatedly made decisions concerning Hagar, God addressed her as someone whose life mattered.
He heard.
He saw.
He spoke.
He provided.
And He preserved her son.
That is not permission to romanticize her suffering.
It is reason to worship a God whose compassion reaches people whom others overlook.
If this story has exposed something in your own heart, do not rush away from that conviction.
Maybe you need to repent of how you have treated someone.
Maybe you need courage to tell the truth about what happened to you.
Maybe you need to stop confusing another person's rejection with God's rejection.
Maybe you need to surrender your life to Jesus Christ for the first time.
Whatever brought you here, do not settle for being emotionally moved by a Bible story while remaining unchanged by the Gospel.
Come to Christ.
Confess your sins.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Receive His grace.
And begin walking in the new life He calls you to live.

And if you have a testimony of how God met you during a season of rejection or hardship, consider sharing it. Your words may encourage someone who has begun to believe that hope is no longer possible.
You do not have to reveal private trauma publicly to prove your faith. Sometimes the bravest prayer is one whispered where only God can hear.
But where it is safe and appropriate, let your testimony remind someone else that they are not alone.

Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, people who have drifted from their faith, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along. Let them encounter Scripture, not merely religious slogans.
And if this ministry has helped you grow in your understanding of God's Word, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Not because you can purchase God's favor.
The Gospel is free. Salvation is a gift of grace. And no monthly payment can replace repentance, faith, obedience, or the generosity God calls us to practice.
Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that giving should be willing rather than compelled (2 Corinthians 9:7).
It can help make room for the next person who is desperately searching for biblical truth at two in the morning.
The next exhausted parent.
The next struggling believer.
The next person carrying guilt who needs to hear that forgiveness is found in Jesus Christ.
The next reader who has never understood why the cross matters.
That is the mission your generosity can help sustain.
Support should come from conviction and freedom, not spiritual pressure.
These are simply ways to express appreciation for those helping the ministry continue. They are not spiritual rewards or measures of faithfulness.
And those free resources matter.
Because biblical nourishment should never be reduced to a transaction.
And if you cannot give or share, you are no less welcome here.
We are not building a community where people must pay to belong.
We are seeking to build a community where Jesus Christ is proclaimed, Scripture is taken seriously, repentance is not avoided, grace is not cheapened, and wounded people are treated with dignity.
Because the point was never to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The point is to make the Gospel known.
And when all the invitations have been made, when the comments have quieted, when the article has disappeared beneath tomorrow's posts, I hope one truth remains with you.
There was a woman in Genesis who did not appear to have much control over her circumstances.
Others made decisions that shaped her life.
Others held authority she did not possess.
Others argued over the consequences.
And twice, the wilderness became part of her story.
But twice, God met her there.
He did not erase the past.
He did not pretend the household had been righteous.
He did not make Hagar the center of the covenant promise that belonged to Isaac.
Yet He saw her.
He heard her.
And He cared for her and her son.
That is the kind of God whose mercy we see unfolding throughout Scripture.
And when we come to Jesus Christ, we encounter the fullest revelation of God's saving love.
The One who knows every sin we have committed and every wound we have carried calls us to repent and believe.
The One who died for sinners offers forgiveness that cannot be earned.
The One who rose from the grave offers a hope stronger than death.
So do not let the failures of Abraham's household distract you from the faithfulness of Abraham's God.
Do not let the cruelty of people convince you that Christ is cruel.
And do not let your own past persuade you that the Savior cannot transform your future.
Hagar's story does not promise that every wilderness will end the way we want.
But it reminds us that suffering does not place a person beyond God's sight.
And the Gospel tells us something even greater.
Through Jesus Christ, sinners can be forgiven, the lost can be reconciled to God, and broken lives can begin to be made new.
They may have written you into a story you never chose, but they do not get to write the final sentence of the life you surrender to Jesus Christ.
